Greeks
grēks
n. pl. (Hellenes; in the New Testament often the Gentile world at large; Greek Hellenes)
From Hellen, the reputed father of the Hellenic race. In apostolic usage the national name widens into a category: everyone who is not a Jew.

Biblical Definition

Greeks in the New Testament rarely means only the inhabitants of Greece. Paired against Jew, it stands for the whole Gentile world — the nations outside the covenant, characterised by their appetite for wisdom as the Jews were characterised by their demand for a sign. Some Greeks were devout worshippers who came up to the feast and asked, “Sir, we would see Jesus.” Others filled the synagogues of the dispersion as God-fearers and became the first harvest of Paul's preaching. The apostle's great antitheses turn on the word: the gospel is to the Jew first and also to the Greek; the Jews require a sign and the Greeks seek after wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, to the Greeks foolishness; and in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek. That last word abolishes not the nations but the wall between them. The Greek is not made a Jew, nor the Jew a Greek; both are made one new man, and the wisdom the Greek sought is found where he would never have looked for it — in a cross.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines Greek as a native of Greece, and notes the language in which the New Testament was written.

expand to see more

GREEK, n. A native of Greece; also, the language of Greece.

2. In Scripture, a Gentile, as opposed to a Jew.

GREEK, a. Pertaining to Greece.

GRECIAN, n. A native of Greece; also, one versed in the Greek language.

The New Testament was originally written in Greek, the common tongue of the eastern empire.

Key Scripture

Joh 12:20 — "And there were certain Greeks among them that came up to worship at the feast:"

Act 17:4 — "And some of them believed, and consorted with Paul and Silas; and of the devout Greeks a great multitude, and of the chief women not a few."

1Co 1:22 — "For the Jews require a sign, and the Greeks seek after wisdom:"

Gal 3:28 — "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus."

Modern Corruption

Galatians 3:28 is lifted out of its argument and made to erase every distinction God has made, when Paul is settling one question only: who may be an heir.

expand to see more

“Neither Jew nor Greek… neither male nor female” has become the proof text for flattening every creational distinction, as though the verse dissolved sex, office, and calling together. Read the chapter and the point is exact. Paul is answering whether a Gentile must become a Jew to inherit Abraham's promise. His answer is that all who are Christ's are Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise — equally, without qualification. The clause concerns standing in Christ and title to the inheritance. The same apostle who wrote it goes on in other letters to order the church by the very distinctions this verse is made to abolish, which is decisive: he did not think he had abolished them.

The recovery is to let the verse do its own enormous work. It is the death of every claim that grace runs along bloodlines, and it is the charter of the Gentile's full sonship. The Greek who once sought wisdom in the schools is now a son and an heir on precisely the same footing as the Jew who once trusted his circumcision — not because the difference between them was declared unreal, but because Christ was made a curse for both.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek Hellen (G1672), a Greek, a Gentile; Hellenistes (G1675), a Grecian Jew; sophia (G4678), wisdom.

expand to see more

Greek Hellen (G1672) — a Greek, and by extension a Gentile; John 12:20, Romans 1:16, 1 Corinthians 1:22.

Greek Hellenistes (G1675) — a Grecian, a Greek-speaking Jew; Acts 6:1, Acts 9:29.

Greek sophia (G4678) — wisdom, the thing the Greeks sought; 1 Corinthians 1:22-24.

Greek moria (G3472) — foolishness, the cross as the Greeks judged it; 1 Corinthians 1:23.

Greek ethnos (G1484) — nation, the wider term for the Gentiles; Matthew 28:19.

Usage

"“The Greeks seek after wisdom” — the national appetite Paul names and confounds."

"“Certain Greeks… came up to worship” — the nations arriving before the Passion."

"“Neither Jew nor Greek” — one title to the inheritance, in Christ."
